misconceptions.statement: The UN is a world government that makes laws all countries must obey.
misconceptions.why: The name 'United Nations' and news of UN 'orders' sound like a ruling authority.
misconceptions.fix: The UN is an organisation of sovereign countries that work together. It cannot pass laws over a country; countries agree to its decisions and treaties.

probe.question: Can the UN pass a law that India must obey like a Parliament law?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, UN laws are above every country's laws.

misconceptions.root_belief: a big organisation at the top must rule everyone
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas about international organisations in civics education

misconceptions.statement: The UN President rules the world.
misconceptions.why: Students map the idea of a country's President or PM onto the UN.
misconceptions.fix: The UN has a Secretary-General who is the chief administrator and voice of the UN, not a ruler. Member countries decide policies.

probe.question: Who is the head ruler of all countries in the UN?
probe.wrong_answer: The UN President.

misconceptions.root_belief: every organisation has a single ruler like a country

misconceptions.statement: The UN has its own big army that it sends to fight wars.
misconceptions.why: Films and news show blue-helmet soldiers and 'UN forces'.
misconceptions.fix: The UN has no standing army. Peacekeeping troops come from member countries on loan for each mission.

probe.question: Where do UN peacekeeping soldiers come from?
probe.wrong_answer: From the UN's own permanent army.

misconceptions.root_belief: visible uniform means a permanent owned force

misconceptions.statement: If the UN says a country must stop, that country is forced to stop.
misconceptions.why: Students assume international bodies have police power like a state.
misconceptions.fix: The UN can only appeal, impose sanctions or authorise action through the Security Council; it cannot directly force a country, so some countries ignore it.

probe.question: Why did a country continue an action despite a UN call to stop?
probe.wrong_answer: Impossible; the UN can force any country to obey.

misconceptions.root_belief: authority always has power to enforce

misconceptions.statement: The UN was formed to fight wars and punish countries.
misconceptions.why: Its link with war news makes it seem like a military alliance.
misconceptions.fix: The UN was set up in 1945 to prevent wars through talks, law and cooperation, and also to help development and human rights.

probe.question: What was the main aim of forming the UN in 1945?
probe.wrong_answer: To fight wars against aggressive countries.

misconceptions.root_belief: peace organisations work mainly through force

misconceptions.statement: The UN headquarters is in Geneva or Delhi, and only a few big countries are members.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse UN offices in Geneva with the headquarters and assume only powerful states join.
misconceptions.fix: The UN headquarters is in New York, with other offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi. Almost every country, 193 in all, is a member.

probe.question: Where is the UN headquarters?
probe.wrong_answer: Geneva.

misconceptions.root_belief: a famous place of work is the main centre

misconceptions.statement: The UN only deals with wars and security, not health or education.
misconceptions.why: News highlights the Security Council more than UN agencies.
misconceptions.fix: Most UN work is on health, children, food, education and climate through agencies like WHO, UNICEF, FAO and UNESCO.

probe.question: Which UN body works for children's health and education?
probe.wrong_answer: None; the UN only handles wars.

misconceptions.root_belief: an institution has one function only

misconceptions.statement: WHO, UNICEF and UNESCO are separate organisations unrelated to the UN.
misconceptions.why: They have their own names and logos.
misconceptions.fix: They are specialised agencies or programmes within the UN system, funded and run with member countries.

probe.question: Is WHO part of the UN system?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is an independent organisation.

misconceptions.root_belief: different names mean unrelated things

misconceptions.statement: In the General Assembly, bigger or richer countries get more votes.
misconceptions.why: Students assume power in the world is mirrored in voting rights.
misconceptions.fix: In the General Assembly each member country, large or small, has one vote.

probe.question: How many votes does India have compared with Bhutan in the General Assembly?
probe.wrong_answer: India has many more votes.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' ideas on voting and equality in civics

misconceptions.statement: The International Court of Justice can punish individual criminals and leaders directly.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up courts for countries with criminal courts.
misconceptions.fix: The ICJ settles legal disputes between countries only, and gives advice to UN organs; it does not try individuals.

probe.question: Does the ICJ try individual leaders as criminals?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it jails them.

misconceptions.root_belief: all courts work the same way

misconceptions.statement: All 15 Security Council members are permanent and have equal power.
misconceptions.why: Students think all members of a council share equal rank.
misconceptions.fix: Only 5 members (US, UK, France, Russia, China) are permanent. 10 others are elected for two-year terms.

probe.question: How many permanent members does the Security Council have?

misconceptions.root_belief: members of a group are all equal

misconceptions.statement: The five permanent members are the five most populous countries.
misconceptions.why: Students guess that size decides a place.
misconceptions.fix: They are the main winners of World War II, chosen in 1945. India, the most populous country, is not one of them.

probe.question: Why is China, but not India, a permanent member?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it has the most people.

misconceptions.root_belief: size or population decides status

misconceptions.statement: A resolution passes if most of the 15 members vote yes, even if one permanent member says no.
misconceptions.why: Students apply simple majority rule from class elections.
misconceptions.fix: A veto by any one of the five permanent members blocks a resolution even if all others agree.

probe.question: 14 members vote yes and 1 permanent member votes no. What happens?
probe.wrong_answer: The resolution passes.

misconceptions.root_belief: majority rule works in every vote
misconceptions.source_hint: civics education research on majority rule assumptions

misconceptions.statement: Everything the UN General Assembly decides is binding on all countries.
misconceptions.why: Students think a vote of nearly all countries must be a command.
misconceptions.fix: General Assembly resolutions are recommendations; only Security Council decisions are legally binding on members.

probe.question: Is a General Assembly resolution legally binding?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, every country must obey it.

misconceptions.root_belief: a decision by many becomes a compulsory law

misconceptions.statement: UN peacekeepers go anywhere and fight to defeat one side.
misconceptions.why: Students think soldiers always fight wars.
misconceptions.fix: Peacekeepers go only with the consent of the host country, stay neutral, and use force mainly in self-defence or to protect civilians.

probe.question: What is the main role of UN peacekeepers?
probe.wrong_answer: To defeat the aggressor in battle.

misconceptions.root_belief: soldiers exist to fight

misconceptions.statement: G20 means 20 countries are members.
misconceptions.why: The number 20 in the name is read literally.
misconceptions.fix: G20 has 19 countries plus the European Union, and the African Union joined in 2023, so 21 members.

probe.question: How many countries are in the G20?
probe.wrong_answer: Exactly 20 countries.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The G20 is a part of the UN and can make laws.
misconceptions.why: Students lump all global bodies together.
misconceptions.fix: The G20 is an informal forum of major economies, separate from the UN, and has no power to make binding laws.

probe.question: Can the G20 pass laws binding its members?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a UN body that makes laws.

misconceptions.root_belief: all global bodies are one system

misconceptions.statement: The G20 includes almost every country in the world.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'world summit' means everybody attends.
misconceptions.fix: The G20 has only about 20 members, but they have around 85 percent of world GDP and two-thirds of the world population.

probe.question: Is Nepal a G20 member?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all countries are members.

misconceptions.root_belief: a world event includes everyone

misconceptions.statement: The G20 summit in India was held in 2023 in Mumbai.
misconceptions.why: Students link big events to well-known cities like Mumbai.
misconceptions.fix: India held the G20 presidency in 2023, and the leaders' summit was held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi in September 2023, with meetings across many cities.

probe.question: In which city was the 2023 G20 leaders' summit?
probe.wrong_answer: Mumbai.

misconceptions.root_belief: the biggest known city hosts big events

misconceptions.statement: India became a permanent G20 member in 2023 because it was host.
misconceptions.why: Hosting is confused with membership.
misconceptions.fix: India was already a member; the presidency rotates among members. In 2023 it was the African Union that was added as a permanent member.

probe.question: Which group joined the G20 at the 2023 Delhi summit?
probe.wrong_answer: India.

misconceptions.root_belief: hosting something means owning it

misconceptions.statement: The G20 2023 theme was about only trade and money.
misconceptions.why: Students think the G20 is a purely financial meeting.
misconceptions.fix: The theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future' covered climate, health, digital public infrastructure, and development along with the economy.

probe.question: What did the G20 2023 theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future' stress?
probe.wrong_answer: Only trade and money.

misconceptions.root_belief: an institution has one function only

misconceptions.statement: Once a country signs an international treaty, no one can ever stop it from breaking it, so treaties are meaningless.
misconceptions.why: Students see news of countries violating agreements.
misconceptions.fix: Treaties are voluntary, and countries follow most of them because of trust, trade and diplomatic cost; some have mechanisms like sanctions or courts.

probe.question: Why do countries usually follow treaties they have signed?
probe.wrong_answer: They do not; treaties have no effect.

misconceptions.root_belief: if rules are broken sometimes they never work

misconceptions.statement: India is a permanent member of the UN Security Council.
misconceptions.why: India's big role and population make it seem permanent.
misconceptions.fix: India is not a permanent member. It has been elected non-permanent member several times and seeks permanent reform of the Council.

probe.question: Does India have veto power in the Security Council?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, India is a permanent member with veto.

misconceptions.root_belief: importance in a field means formal status

misconceptions.statement: India joined the UN only recently, after becoming a big economy.
misconceptions.why: Students link global roles to recent economic news.
misconceptions.fix: India was a founding member in 1945, even before independence, and has sent peacekeepers to many UN missions.

probe.question: When did India become a UN member?
probe.wrong_answer: In the 1990s after liberalisation.

misconceptions.root_belief: present importance means recent beginning
